data.title: Anthropic's IPO: How many times did investors actually earn?
data.description:
Author｜Curry, Deep Tide TechFlow

The capital market witnessed an extremely rare transfer of interests.

Based on the offering price of $83, Anthropic's fully diluted valuation firmly stood above $1.4 trillion. Over the past five years, various capital sources have poured $142.3 billion into this company, which, at the moment of listing, swelled into a total holding value of a full $861.1 billion.

In five years, the overall return multiple exceeded 6 times.

In this period rife with asset valuation bubbles and computing power anxiety, Anthropic delivered a nearly trillion-dollar check to all Silicon Valley investors with a hefty prospectus. However, looking back along the timeline, you'll find that this largest revenue-sharing feast in history didn't follow the usual patterns.

Angel's Bet and Gambler's Chips: No Reputable VCs in the First Two Rounds

Now everyone wants a seat on Anthropic's shareholder list, but in its first two years when it needed money most, almost all mainstream Silicon Valley venture capital firms were absent.

In May 2021, Anthropic completed a $124 million Series A funding round. The lead investor wasn't Sequoia Capital or Andreessen Horowitz, but Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, with Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt also contributing. It was an angel round purely backed by tech old money and tech enthusiasts. At the time, Anthropic's share price was only $0.257. Based on the offering price of $83, these early investors received an astonishing 322.5-fold return. The $120 million initially invested is now worth over $40.3 billion. Even more surreal than the Series A funding round was the Series B round in April 2022. At that time, the big model hadn't yet seen the explosive growth of ChatGPT, and Anthropic's security research was considered by most mainstream venture capitalists as a money-burning laboratory project with no prospect of commercialization. In this $982 million funding round, the lead investor was the then-powerful crypto giant SBF and his FTX. SBF alone signed checks for $500 million. If calculated based on a price of $83, the return for Series B investors was a staggering 73.9 times, making FTX's holdings worth a full $37 billion on the day of its IPO. This should have been a textbook example of a phenomenal success in venture capital history. However, fate played a cruel trick on this failing exchange. In early 2024, to raise funds to repay creditors, FTX's bankruptcy liquidation team hastily sold its Anthropic shares for $1.34 billion to a group of buyers, including Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund MGX and SBF's former parent company, Jane Street Capital. The liquidators touted this transaction as a major victory in debt resolution. Until today, as the clock struck midnight, the truth finally came out: the liquidation team had sold off nearly $35.7 billion. If they had held onto this stake, FTX could have had two to three hundred billion dollars left over after fully repaying all creditors' principal and interest on Anthropic alone. SBF bet on the highest-returning technology asset of this era, but its own misappropriation of client funds brought it to its knees just short of dawn. The Big Players' Overt Strategy While SBF exited with regret and early angel investors awaited their dividends, the true catalyst for this wealth feast was the entry of two tech giants with their own product offerings and computing power. Among the entire investor list, Amazon holds the largest single entity with unrealized gains. Amazon invested approximately $18 billion, the vast majority in the form of convertible notes, locking in a conversion cost of around $2 per share. Compared to the offering price of $83, this investment yielded a paper return of over 16 times. Amazon held approximately 21% of Anthropic's shares, with a book value of nearly $290 billion on the day of the IPO. Google was not to be outdone. Through early convertible bonds and subsequent capital injections, the value of Google's shares soared to approximately $78 billion. Together, the two cloud giants took nearly $370 billion from Anthropic's market capitalization, accounting for almost half of the entire IPO's gains. Even more remarkably, these large companies never just profited from equity. While its equity has expanded, Anthropic has signed long-term agreements to purchase over $110 billion in computing power from Amazon AWS and over $111 billion from Google Cloud. These giants have not only reaped returns on their investments by more than ten times, but have also conveniently pre-sold out their future data center computing power in full under irrevocable contracts. Faced with the dual calculations of capital and business, these large companies have truly won twice. Venture capitalists are lining up to carry the load, and the chips are no longer cheap. As for those top venture capitalists who are slow to react, they can only act as the loaders in this relay race, with valuations constantly rising. In May 2023, Spark Capital led the Series C funding round, achieving a return of approximately 74 times. They subsequently participated in every subsequent round, investing a total of $777 million, which has now yielded a substantial return of over $10 billion. In early 2024, Menlo Ventures led the Series D round, achieving a return of approximately 28 times. In 2025, Lightspeed Venture Partners led the Series E round, with the return narrowing to 15 times. The further along the funding round, the more astonishing the premium becomes. By February of this year, when GIC and Coatue led the Series G funding round, the investment multiple had shrunk to 3.2 times; when Sequoia Capital and other established giants took over the Series H round in May, their entry cost was as high as $58.9 per share, and by the time of the IPO, the unrealized profit was only 1.4 times. Venture capitalists broke their original valuation red lines, queuing up to fund at valuations in the hundreds of billions of dollars, essentially using expensive tickets to provide a final liquidity guarantee for early-stage geeks, gamblers, and large companies. Besides capital, this wealth redistribution also fell on the shoulders of ordinary workers. Anthropic's seven co-founders each held approximately 240 million shares, equivalent to a net worth of about $20 billion; all employees and the technology team shared stock and option incentives worth approximately $335 billion, creating the most spectacular employee wealth creation in the tech industry since the early days of Google. From a mere 25-cent agreement to a trillion-dollar empire worth $83, Anthropic's profit-sharing chart is a testament to Silicon Valley's most authentic survival philosophy. It proves that when a technological wave arrives, advanced knowledge can yield hundreds of times the profit, and it also proves that giants can easily devour most of the achievements through infrastructure. But perhaps the most profound footnote it leaves for the market is still that of the young man, SBF, who was arrested in the Bahamas. In the game of capital, having a good hand doesn't guarantee victory; only those who survive to sit in the chair and cash in their chips deserve to enjoy this feast.

data.title: Could Rene Haas Take Over Nvidia? What Would It Mean for Crypto?
data.description:
Nvidia could be approaching a major leadership transition, with Rene Haas emerging as a potential successor to Jensen Huang. The Arm CEO is no stranger to the chipmaker, having previously led its computing products business before helping turn Arm into a major player in the global AI infrastructure market.

— Polymarket (@Polymarket) November 16, 2026

Haas’s possible move comes as Nvidia sits at the center of the AI boom, with its data center business generating billions in quarterly revenue. If he takes the helm, his experience expanding Arm’s role in AI computing could shape Nvidia’s next phase of growth — with potential implications for technology stocks, Bitcoin, and the wider AI-focused crypto sector.

Rene Haas Could Bring His AI Infrastructure Experience to Nvidia

Haas is not an outsider stepping into unfamiliar territory. He spent seven years at Nvidia, leading its computing products business between 2006 and 2013, before moving to Arm. He became Arm’s CEO in 2022 and has since helped expand the company’s position in the growing AI infrastructure market.

Under his leadership, Arm reported $4.92 billion in revenue for fiscal 2026, up from $4.01 billion the previous year. The company’s technology already reaches more than 99% of smartphones worldwide, while its chip designs also support infrastructure used by major cloud providers and Nvidia itself.

— NVIDIA Newsroom (@nvidianewsroom) November 17, 2026

That experience could prove valuable if Haas takes over Nvidia. Rather than focusing solely on the chips powering the AI boom, he could look to expand the company’s broader computing ecosystem, including data center infrastructure and integrated AI platforms.

However, Nvidia would give Haas a very different challenge from the one he faced at Arm. The company is already one of the most influential players in the AI industry, meaning its next chief executive would inherit an enormous business with considerable expectations to maintain its growth.

Nvidia’s AI Dominance Could Give Its Next CEO a Powerful Starting Point

Nvidia’s latest financial results illustrate the scale of the business Haas could potentially inherit. The company reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, with its data center division contributing $107.6 billion. Overall revenue climbed 103% year over year, highlighting the enormous demand for the computing infrastructure behind the AI industry.

The company is also moving into its next generation of hardware, with its Vera Rubin platform entering production and beginning to ship. These developments give Nvidia’s next leader a substantial foundation as the company looks to maintain its position in an increasingly competitive AI market.

If Haas brings some of the strategies he pursued at Arm to Nvidia, the company could place greater emphasis on integrated computing platforms, data center infrastructure, and new AI applications. Such a direction could help sustain investment across the broader AI ecosystem, although the exact priorities of a potential new CEO remain uncertain.

Nvidia’s succession process is still ongoing. The company has reportedly engaged executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles, which approached Haas as part of its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang. However, the outreach does not mean Haas has agreed to take the position or that Nvidia has made a final decision.

Could a New Nvidia Era Give Crypto an AI Boost?

The potential impact of a Haas appointment would not necessarily stop at the semiconductor industry. Nvidia’s performance has become an important part of the broader AI investment narrative, while Bitcoin and Ethereum have increasingly moved alongside technology stocks as investors shift between risk-on and risk-off assets.

If a new leadership strategy helps sustain confidence in AI spending, the resulting optimism could spill over into other risk assets, including cryptocurrencies. However, that would be an indirect market effect rather than evidence that a change at Nvidia would automatically push Bitcoin or Ethereum higher.

AI-focused crypto projects could also attract attention if demand for computing infrastructure continues to grow. Networks such as Render, Bittensor, Artificial Superintelligence Alliance, and Akash are exploring different ways to connect decentralized infrastructure with GPU resources, distributed computing, and AI development.

Greater investment in AI could create opportunities for these projects by keeping demand for computing resources in focus. But increased spending by Nvidia and other centralized technology companies would not automatically translate into greater usage or token demand for decentralized networks.
